text:
Dear Dr. Reynolds,

Thank you for seeing Leo Davies, a five-year-old boy referred for assessment of progressive gait and strength difficulties over the past several months. 

His parents note that he has experienced marked trouble running alongside classmates at preschool and suffers from repeated falls and stumbling. He lives at home with both parents, has normal speech and social development, and takes only a daily pediatric multivitamin. Family history is negative for early-onset motor or neuromuscular disorders.

On physical examination, Leo is alert and cooperative. Cranial nerves II through XII are intact. Motor testing reveals diminished strength across his proximal limb girdles, as well as bilateral weakness during ankle dorsiflexion. Inspection of his lower extremities reveals exaggerated, high-arched feet. Furthermore, sensory and reflex testing revealed distinct signs of a peripheral neuropathy. 

Electrodiagnostic evaluation was initiated: needle electromyography demonstrated distinct myopathic motor unit potentials, whereas conduction velocities on nerve testing were entirely preserved. A screening echocardiogram confirmed that ventricular function is normal with no structural lesions. He displays no respiratory distress, maintains oxygen saturations of 99% on ambient air, and his chest is clear to auscultation. 

Given these mixed neuromuscular features, I would be grateful for your comprehensive clinical assessment and advice on subsequent diagnostic steps.

Warm regards,

Dr. Arthur Vance
Department of Pediatrics, St. Jude Community Health
